sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Today we are going back to the very beginning — the first page of the Bible. Before there were nations, kings, or prophets, before there was a single person on the earth, there was God. The book of Genesis opens with ten simple words that answer one of the biggest questions anyone can ask: where did everything come from?

Genesis chapter one, verse one says: “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.”

Notice that the Bible doesn't begin by trying to prove that God exists. It simply starts with Him. God is the main character of this story, and of every story that follows. As we listen today, let's ask three questions. What does this story tell us about God? What does it tell us about the world? And what does it tell us about ourselves?

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
The Bible says that in the beginning, the earth was without form, and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. Picture it: no light, no shape, no life. Just deep, dark waters.

Then God spoke. “And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.” That's all it took. No struggle, no tools, no raw materials. God simply said it, and it happened. God saw the light, that it was good, and He divided the light from the darkness. He called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.

On the second day, God made the firmament — the wide expanse of the sky — to separate the waters above from the waters below.

On the third day, God gathered the waters together into one place, and dry land appeared. He called the dry land Earth and the waters Seas. Then He told the earth to bring forth grass, plants that yield seed, and trees that bear fruit. Think of every apple, every oak tree, every blade of grass in your yard. They all trace back to that third day.

On the fourth day, God placed lights in the sky: the greater light to rule the day — the sun — and the lesser light to rule the night — the moon. And the Bible adds, almost in passing, “he made the stars also.” Billions of stars, and Scripture mentions them in just a few words. That tells us something about how great God is.

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
On the fifth day, God filled the seas with living creatures — great whales and every kind of fish — and He filled the sky with birds. And God blessed them and told them to be fruitful and multiply.

On the sixth day, God made the animals of the land: cattle, creeping things, and wild beasts, each after its kind. And then God did something different. Up to this point He had said, “Let there be,” and “Let the earth bring forth.” But now God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness.”

Genesis chapter one, verse twenty-seven tells us: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.”

Chapter two zooms in to show us how closely God was involved. God formed the man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul. God planted a garden eastward in Eden and put the man there to tend it and keep it. God brought the animals to Adam to see what he would name them. But among all the animals, there was not found a helper suitable for him. So God caused a deep sleep to fall on Adam, took one of his ribs, and made a woman, and brought her to the man. Adam was overjoyed. Here at last was someone like him.

At the end of the sixth day, “God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.” Not just good — very good.

Then came the seventh day. God had finished His work, and He rested. Not because He was tired — God never grows weary — but to set a pattern. Genesis chapter two, verse three says: “And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made.”

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
So what does this story teach us?

First, it teaches us that God is the Creator, and that He is powerful. He spoke, and the universe came to be. If God can do that, then nothing you face today is too big for Him.

Second, it teaches us that the world is good, and that it belongs to God. We are not owners; we are caretakers. Adam was placed in the garden to tend it and keep it. Caring for the world around us — our homes, our land, our animals — is part of honoring the One who made it.

Third, it teaches us that every person has great worth. Only human beings are described as made in the image of God. That includes you. It also includes the coworker who frustrates you, the neighbor who's hard to love, the child, the elderly, the stranger. When we treat people with respect and kindness, we are honoring the image of God in them.

And fourth, it teaches us the gift of rest. God built a rhythm into creation: work, and then rest. In a busy world that never stops, taking time to rest, to worship, and to be with the people we love is not laziness. It is following God's own example.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
Let's take a moment to reflect. Think about one thing in creation that amazes you — a sunrise, the ocean, a newborn baby, the stars at night. Thank God for it.

Let's pray. Heavenly Father, You are the Creator of heaven and earth. Thank You for the beauty of the world You made, and thank You for making me in Your image. Help me to care for Your creation, to treat every person with dignity, and to rest in You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. Next time, we'll continue the story with Noah and the great flood.
